en: The Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai explains the "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs. Regarding this parable of the medicinal herbs,
although it fully contains mountains, rivers, clouds, and rain, the title is designated solely by the term "medicinal herbs" because the land...

The clouds and rain are that which produce and moisten; the grasses and trees are that which are produced and moistened. While all things produced and moistened have their utility, the medicinal herbs possess the strongest efficacy. Likewise, all conditioned wholesome dharmas (*sāsrava-kuśala*) are capable of eliminating evil, yet the unconditioned (*anāsrava*) is supreme. Among the assembly of those with the unconditioned, the four great disciples understood the Buddha’s profound intent through these parables. The Buddha praised them, saying, "Excellent! This is most rare," and described their attainment of understanding by means of these metaphors for those individuals; therefore, this is called the "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs" chapter.

When medicinal herbs have grown for a long time, upon receiving the nourishment of clouds and rain, they flourish and spread with brilliant splendor; their sprouts and stems grow lushly on the outside, while their vital energy and moisture fill them within. This is analogous to those dwelling in the final body of the stage of no-outflows (anāsrava) who abide in *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* and no longer aspire to the unsurpassed Buddha-way.

Now, having heard this sutra, they realize their own vehicle—the Buddha-vehicle—and simultaneously transport others. As the text says, "Today we are truly śrāvakas"; by the sound of the Buddha-way, they cause all to hear, possessing superior power and function both internally and externally, for themselves and for others. Therefore, it is called the "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs" chapter.

As for medicinal herbs, they can eliminate the wind and cold disorders of the four great elements, nourish the five viscera, restore youth, and arrest the signs of aging; yet now, having encountered the clouds and rain, they have suddenly become the King of Medicines, and by ingesting them, all manner of ailments are universally cured and the body is transformed into that of an immortal. This is analogous to those without outflows hearing this sutra: they shatter the delusions of ignorance and open up the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. As the text says: "Today we are truly the sons of the Buddha; this unsurpassed treasury of jewels we obtained without seeking. Whatever a son of the Buddha ought to obtain, they have already obtained it; they have received their prediction of enlightenment face-to-face before the Buddha. To celebrate this excellence while acknowledging its subtlety, it is therefore called the "Parable of the Medicinal Herbs" chapter.
The first section is the master and disciple’s exposition of the meaning of the world-siddhānta;
the next section, which generates wholesome states, is for the benefit of others;
and the subsequent section concerns the two siddhāntas of remedial therapy and the ultimate truth.
This is called the "Chapter on the Explanation of Causes and Conditions.

The remaining aspects—namely, the provisional teaching, the fundamental and the trace, and the contemplation of the mind—may be understood by applying this same principle; they are not recorded here at length.
This chapter is the third section of the parables, which provides a formal exposition.
The older commentary states:
"It expounds thirteen verses praising the profound kindness of the Buddha, and further explains the teachings through the metaphor of a person, with phrasing that is both subtle and skillful."
The Master said:

"One should not be partial in this regard. The Sūtra speaks of the Tathāgata’s true merits as being 'well-expounded,' and it fully describes his mastery of both the provisional and the ultimate; the clear evidence for this is found right here.
The thirteen verses merely represent the teaching shared with the Two Vehicles to acknowledge their gratitude; the analogy of the person acting as a guide is simply the Buddha’s provisional merit."

Now, to speak of "comprehensively recounting" means to fully understand [the Master's deeds] from the initial karmic connection through his natural disposition, through the intermediate period of pursuit and guidance, and finally to the entrustment of the Dharma-treasure; thus, one comes to know the immeasurable and boundless virtues and graces, both subtle and manifest.
The text consists of two parts:
first, a brief exposition of its establishment; second, an extensive exposition of its establishment.
The brief exposition, in turn, has two sections:
First, the dual praise of "Excellent" (*sādhu*); second, acknowledging what was not yet fully understood.

Regarding the dual praise: one "Excellent" praises his acknowledgment of the reality (*tattva*) in both instances, and one "Excellent" praises his acknowledgment of the provisional (*upāya*) in both instances.

Regarding the phrase “skillfully expounding the Tathāgata’s true merits,” “true” (zhēnshí) refers to the ultimate reality (*tattva*), while “merits” (gōngdé) refers to the provisional means (*upāya*).

Furthermore, the *Avataṃsaka* is intended to lead one toward the realization of reality; the Tripiṭaka guides by leading through the provisional; the Vaipulya sutras inspire faith; and the *Prajñāpāramitā* leads through the teachings—all of these encompass both the provisional and the real. Only the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, in its entrustment of the treasure, discusses reality exclusively.
Because his expressions were refined and skillful, he was said to have "spoken well"; because all [his words] were the Buddha-dharma, they were said to be "true.
"It is exactly as you have said" is the meaning of a seal of confirmation.
Furthermore, from the passage "The Tathāgata further possesses... onwards, it describes that which his comprehension does not reach.
How is it that he does not reach it?
It means that he does not reach [the states of] regression and progression, horizontal and vertical, both horizontal and vertical, or neither horizontal nor vertical.

Why is this? The great cloud covers all universally, bearing a pervasive coolness; the heavy rain moistens everything equally, so that none fail to receive its bounty. It causes the entire world to perceive and know the unprecedented Dharma; why then would you suddenly teach only the two vehicles in unison, allowing them to receive benefit alone?
Not speaking of humans and devas as mere small grasses is what is meant by "retrogression beyond reach.

Bodhisattvas are called "superior grass," and are also called "small trees" and "great trees"; they flourish and grow luxuriantly, benefiting both themselves and others, yet they do not take pride in this—this is what is meant by "advancement beyond reach."

Furthermore, since all ten dharma realms equally constitute the Buddha-dharma realm, why do you suddenly restrict its scope to only the two vehicles, while remaining entirely silent regarding the other eight dharma realms?
This constitutes a horizontal deficiency in your understanding.

Furthermore, the seven stages of expedient means (*saptavidha-upāya*) proceed from the shallow to the deep, all entering into ultimate reality; the other five expedient means are not mentioned at all, which constitutes being "incomparable in the vertical dimension.
Moreover, its benefit to the three periods of time has never been suspended for even a moment, which constitutes being "incomparable both in the horizontal and the vertical dimensions."

Now, as for the mountains, rivers, valleys, and so forth, these collectively refer to the single earth. This single earth is capable of producing all things without ever discriminating between one thing and another, nor excluding some while favoring others. Seeds of grasses and trees all rely upon this earth and have no other support. When a single cloud gathers and darkens, its moisture is dense everywhere; when it rains with a single flavor, it makes no distinction between the withered and the flourishing. Since the universal moistening is the same, all things equally attain growth. The Tathāgata’s equality is likewise inconceivable. Truly, he does not first act suddenly and later gradually, nor is there a distinction between the beginning, middle, and end. It is like a dragon raising auspicious clouds that rain universally upon all things: though the rain does not fall upon bodies and minds where it is not needed, those who receive it are freed from heat and attain coolness. This is the equality, vastness, profundity, breadth, and distance of the five vehicles and seven expedient means throughout the ten directions and three periods of time—it is inconceivable and without differentiation. This is what is neither horizontal nor vertical, beyond the reach of the senses.

The meaning of "not reaching" is not that it is entirely and suddenly negated; rather, it is simply because one looks back from a later state of mind to an earlier one, and since the ultimate ground has not yet been exhausted, it is said to be "inexhaustible.

Furthermore, the initial realization of the letter *A* also possesses the merits of the subsequent letter *Ta*; however, while the understanding according to the teaching reaches as far as *A*, there has not yet been the opportunity to advance to a comprehensive mastery of both the horizontal and vertical dimensions.
Furthermore, it is appropriate that a Bodhisattva practicing through skillful means should act in this manner.
The extensive exposition consists of two parts: prose and verse.
The prose section also has two parts:
first, the exposition establishing the opening of three and the manifestation of one; second, from "You, Kāśyapa," onwards, the concluding praise.
The first part consists of the Dharma, the analogy, and their synthesis.
Within the Dharma there are further two parts:
first, the preliminary citation of the "Dharma King," which serves to encourage faith without falsehood;
second, from the passage beginning with "In all dharmas" onwards, the actual exposition of the opening of the three and the manifestation of the one.
Just as a noble lady has no fear externally and no duplicity internally, so too is the Dharma King:
all evils have been exhausted, and his speech is truthful and sincere.
The old [translation] says:
The preceding section described how the teachings of those of medium capacity are not in vain, thereby encouraging those of inferior capacity to accept them with faith.
Now it is said:

although the Buddha-dharma is vast, it does not transcend the provisional and the real; beyond the provisional and the real, there is no other teaching. Yet, the claim that these are "immeasurable" is difficult for the mind to believe. Therefore, the title of "Dharma King" is invoked to encourage faith, and this serves as the basis for the subsequent analogy of the great cloud.
From "Regarding all phenomena" onwards, the opening of the provisional and the revelation of the real are elucidated in terms of the teaching.
From "The Tathāgata contemplates and knows" onwards, the opening of the provisional and the revelation of the real are elucidated in terms of wisdom.
The two teachings manifest the two wisdoms, and the two wisdoms expound the two teachings; thus, wisdom and teaching mutually accomplish one another.
"All dharmas" refers to the seven stages of expedient means, which constitute the horizontal dimension;
in contrast to the single reality, they constitute the vertical dimension.

If you say this is not so, why is it that after first resolving upon the Great Mind in the presence of twenty trillion Buddhas, one subsequently adopts the Lesser Vehicle, wanders through the five destinies, and yet possesses all ten dharma realms—even as a single person—let alone those at the seven stages of the expedient means?

Although these teachings are numerous, they are fully illuminated by the *upāya-pāramitā* (perfection of skillful means) such that nothing remains unexhausted; it accords with the sounds of each category to ensure that every teaching meets its purpose. For humans and devas, it teaches the precepts and wholesome deeds; for those of the Two Vehicles, it teaches the Truths and Conditions; for those of the Tripiṭaka, it teaches phenomena and the perfections (*pāramitās*); for those of the Shared Teaching, it teaches non-arising; and for those of the Distinct Teaching, it teaches the sequential revelation of the *tathāgatagarbha*. This is called "describing the threefold opening of the reception."
From the passage "The Dharma he preached" onwards, the text describes the manifestation of the ultimate reality (*tattva*) according to the teaching.

"Ground" (*bhūmi*) refers to the true aspect of reality (*dharmatā*). It is called "one" (*eka*) because it is ultimately non-dual; it is called "all" (*sarva*) because its nature is vast and expansive; it is called "wisdom" (*jñāna*) because it is quiescent yet ever-illuminating; and it is called "ground" because it serves as the non-abiding foundation upon which all phenomena are established. This is the definitive exposition of the Perfect Teaching (*pūrṇa-yāna*).

Everything that has been taught is intended to lead all sentient beings to this stage of wisdom; these texts revealing the truth are as radiant as the sun—how can you sleep through them in ignorance and form other interpretations?

For example, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* (Dapin) extensively enumerates all dharmas as being the Mahāyāna; "yāna" (vehicle) is the Great Vehicle, the vehicle is the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), and the true mark is the stage of omniscience (*sarvajñatā-bhūmi*). The preceding passage states, "Only this one thing is real," which refers to this stage; "the other two are not true" refers to the seven stages of expedient means (*saptopāya-kauśalya*).
This section, based on the two teachings of gradual and sudden, describes the revelation of the provisional to manifest the real.
From the passage "The Tathāgata contemplates and knows all dharmas" onwards, it describes the revelation of the provisional to manifest the real from the perspective of wisdom.
"Contemplating all that is returned to and sought" is the illumination of the provisional;

"ultimate clarity" is the illumination of the real. Since the two wisdoms illuminate the two spheres—the partial and the perfect—without obstruction or hindrance, they are able to expound the two teachings of the provisional and the real; this cites wisdom to explain the teaching.

"Knowing where one is headed" is the medicine for consciousness; "the practice of the profound mind" is the knowledge of the illness. Both the illness and the medicine are provisional teachings (*upāya-dharma*). Each provisional teaching has its own destination: precepts, goodness, and so forth, lead proximately to the realms of humans and devas; yet if they function as conditions, lowering the head and raising the hand leads distantly to the fruit of Buddhahood.

The foundations of mindfulness (*smṛty-upasthāna*) and the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) lead proximately to *nirvāṇa*; yet if they serve as the adornment of merit, the path you practice is that of a bodhisattva, leading distantly to the Precious Place.
Even regarding the six perfections and other general or specific dharmas, it is understandable that their proximate and distant destinations follow different paths.

Furthermore, the precepts and wholesome deeds are the medicine for humans and devas; the truths, conditions, and liberations are the medicine for those of the three vehicles; even the "penetrating" and "distinctive" [samādhis] may be understood in this way.
Regarding "the practices of the profound mind," there are two kinds:
the profound mind that clings to the environment and its inhabitants (the *āśraya* and *adhiṣṭhāna*), and the profound mind that clings to the dharmas one grasps.
Attachment to the primary and secondary [realms] gives rise to the profound and heavy ten evil deeds that obstruct the vehicle of humans and devas;

attachment to the dharmas one upholds gives rise to the four inversions, the three paths, the six obscurations, the four abodes, the five abodes, and so forth, which obstruct the various vehicles of the noble ones.
One should know that the manifestations of deep-seated mental afflictions are diverse; through the illumination of expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*), one penetrates them all without obstruction.
Furthermore, "thoroughly investigating and clearly understanding all phenomena" refers to what is illuminated by ultimate wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*).

All provisional dharmas enter into reality; therefore, it is called "ultimate. Because it is that which is known by true wisdom, it is called "comprehended"; because it is that which is seen by the Buddha-eye, it is called "clear."

If this wisdom illuminates this medicine and this illness, but does not illuminate that medicine and that illness, and if that wisdom illuminates those but cannot illuminate these—such that their types and categories differ—this is the illumination of provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*).
If a single wisdom universally illuminates all medicines and all illnesses, this is the illumination of ultimate wisdom (*tattva-jñāna*).
Because it can demonstrate such a perfect realm and wisdom to sentient beings, it is called "all-encompassing wisdom" (*sarvajñajñāna*).

Furthermore, "all phenomena" (*sarvadharma*) refers to the ten dharma-realms; since each of these ten realms has distinct characteristics and desires, the resulting retributions and destinations they reach are likewise different.
To know that all phenomena are exhausted is called "knowing the illness"; to know all that is clung to by the deep mind is called "knowing the medicine.

There are varying depths of medicine; as the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "The wisdom of suchness knows the mind of greed, the mind of hatred, and the mind of delusion. To know through the wisdom of suchness is called "knowing the deep mind. To penetrate reality according to principle without obstruction—whether it be the medicines of all dharmas such as precepts, goodness, truths, conditions, or the perfections—and to know them all through the wisdom of suchness, is called "penetrating without hindrance."
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "unimpeded penetration" within the section on expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*), it discusses the real (*tattva*) by way of the expedient;
within the section on real wisdom (*tattva-jñāna*), the phrase "regarding all dharmas" discusses the expedient by way of the real.

Regarding the mutual manifestation of the two aspects: this clarifies that the real is indeed the provisional and the provisional is indeed the real. One should know that, ultimately, it is neither provisional nor real, neither differentiated nor non-differentiated; for while there is differentiation through the provisional application of wisdom and skillful means, once one reaches the stage of ultimate wisdom, there is no differentiation.
It is like the earth, which makes no distinction between various plants and trees; though they appear diverse, there is no diversity in them, nor is there diversity within that which is non-diverse.

Furthermore, it is as when one discusses the Dharma based on the mind, or discusses the mind based on the Dharma: the mind possesses various enumerations, while the Dharma possesses no enumerations. Yet the mind does not depart from the Dharma, nor does the Dharma depart from the mind; it is merely a matter of numbering what is unnumbered, and being unnumbered within what is numbered.
The provisional and the ultimate are also like this, and so forth.
From "For example" onwards is the second section, the explanation by way of analogy.
This text consists of two parts:
The first part is an illustrative exposition, and the latter is a restatement of the core doctrine followed by praise.
The illustration consists of an opening and a closing.
The opening is divided into two parts:
First, the analogy of differentiation illustrates the aforementioned provisional teachings and provisional wisdom;
second, the analogy of non-differentiation illustrates the aforementioned ultimate teachings and ultimate wisdom.
The three types of grass and two types of trees differ in their fineness and density; therefore, they are said to be distinct.
Yet, because they are all supported and moistened by a single earth and a single rain, there is no distinction between them.
If one observes only their branches and twigs, one might say that each is different.
If one investigates the source of their flourishing, it is none other than the earth and rain.

Internally, this corresponds to the fact that while the provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*) illuminates the seven-five [categories] as distinct, the ultimate wisdom (*tattva-jñāna*) shines upon them so that they ultimately return to the single reality (*eka-tattva*). Thus, the single reality is the seven-five, and the seven-five is the single reality; there is differentiation within non-differentiation, and non-differentiation within differentiation, and so forth.
There are six analogies for the distinctions:
first, the land; second, the herbs and trees; third, the dense clouds; fourth, the falling rain; fifth, receiving moisture; and sixth, growth.

First, regarding the analogy of the land: the ancient [text] generally mentions the lands of the three thousandfold world system, then specifically distinguishes the mountains, rivers, valleys, and gullies as the causes for the practice of the five vehicles. The valley, which receives much water, is likened to the bodhisattva; the stream is likened to the pratyekabuddha; the river is likened to the śrāvaka; and the mountain, which receives little moisture, is likened to the human and celestial vehicles.

Now, it is said that the conditioning cause (*hetu-pratyaya*) should be illustrated by the analogy of a seed being moistened and growing; whereas although the land, mountains, and rivers may receive moisture, they lack the two meanings of "seed" and "growth.

Furthermore, the subsequent passage synthesizing the analogies states, "Pervading the world of devas, humans, and asuras," and the verse says, "Among all the assemblies of devas and humans"; in neither case are the land and so forth used as analogies for the conditioning cause. Therefore, they are not employed here.

Now, the "great trichiliocosm" is used as a metaphor for the world of sentient beings, while the "mountains, rivers, valleys, and lands" are used as a metaphor for the world of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).
There is no separate entity apart from a world that is not composed of mountains, rivers, valleys, and lands;
likewise, there is no separate entity apart from sentient beings that is not composed of the five aggregates.

The land being pervasive serves as a metaphor for the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*); the mountains, rivers, valleys, and gullies serve as metaphors for the other four aggregates. Although the dependent vegetation—such as grasses and trees—relies upon the land and so forth, the land is not identical to the vegetation. The substance and trunk of the vegetation are merely called "grass and trees," yet the seeds of these plants have no separate name; one simply takes their capacity to produce as "seeds," and that which they produce as the substance and trunk as "grass and trees. All are planted with roots in the earth, and thus the earth is the foundation.

Internally, this corresponds to the cause of habituation and the fruit of habituation; although these depend upon the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), the five aggregates themselves are not identical to the cause and fruit. It is by depending upon the aggregates that the cause of habituation exists, and its growth and fulfillment is termed the fruit of habituation.
When effects and causes arise based on the aggregates (*skandha*), this is illustrated by the analogy of mountains, rivers, and lands;
when seeds of grasses and trees receive moisture and grow, this is illustrated by the complete formation [of these features].

Furthermore, to clarify another specific analogy: although mountains are high and steep, they possess five characteristics such as depressions and elevations; even though land is level, it likewise possesses five characteristics such as mounds and ponds. These correspond to the five characteristics of the five vehicles and the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
Mountains are like the five aggregates (*skandha*) of a bodhisattva; rivers are like pratyekabuddhas; streams are like śrāvakas; the land is like the heavens; and the low valleys are like humans.

Each of the five aggregates serves as the basis for the causes and fruits of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), just as mountains, rivers, streams, valleys, and land all serve as the basis for seeds, roots, trunks, and so forth.
Furthermore, the "trichiliocosm" is used as an analogy for the principle of the true cause, serving as the universal basis for all things;
"mountains, rivers, valleys, and the land" are analogies for the form and mind that constitute the retributive fruits of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases of sentient beings;
and "grass, trees, thickets, and forests" are analogies for the habitual causes of sentient beings.

These three dharmas are inseparable; their practice relies upon the aggregates (skandhas) and the sense bases (āyatanas), yet the aggregates and sense bases do not transcend the nature of phenomena (dharmatā). It is as when grasses and trees rely upon mountains and rivers, and mountains and rivers rely upon the world, and so forth.
The six characters are perfectly distinct; how can they be interpreted [as you suggest]?
Furthermore, since the sequence is such, why would one intermingle the scriptural text and excerpt it out of order?
From the phrase "the grasses and trees that grow" onwards is the second section: the analogy of the grasses and trees that grow.
"Herb" (*huì*) is the general name for grasses; "tree" (*mù*) is the collective term for trees.
A multitude of grasses forms a thicket; a multitude of trees forms a forest.

That which possesses superior efficacy in curing illness is called "medicine" (*yào*); just as within the wholesome dharmas all can remedy evil, the untainted (*anāsrava*) wholesome dharma excels in its capacity to cure afflictions.

Among the lower category of herbs and trees, the forest trees have broad canopies of branches and trunks and provide great utility; therefore, they are used as a metaphor for the two types of bodhisattvas.
As for "various kinds," this refers to the seeds of the causes and effects of the five vehicles and the seven wholesome practices; hence, the term "various" is used.
That which consists of the various designations for each category is "name" (*nāman*); that which consists of their respective essential characteristics is "form" (*rūpa*).
From the phrase "dense clouds" (*mimyun*) downward is the third section: the analogy of dense clouds.

The clouds possess form and color and provide cover and shade; the subsequent passage mentions "thunder resounding afar. Here, the cover and shade are a metaphor for the Buddha’s compassion, the form and color are a metaphor for the Buddha’s manifestation in the world, and the thunder is a metaphor for the Buddha’s verbal teachings.
"Mystic Cloud" (*mimyun*) refers to the three mysteries: compassion is the mystery of mind, form and color are the mystery of body, and the sound of thunder is the mystery of speech.
"Pervasively spread" (*mibubu*) means everywhere; because it is both mystic and pervasive, it is called "pervasively spread."
Pervaded by compassion, the response-body (nirmāṇakāya) preaches the Dharma throughout the ten dharma-realms; thus it is said to be "pervasively spread.
The *Scriptures and Vinaya of Various Characteristics* states:
"Clouds have five colors: those that are blue have much wind; those that are red have much fire; those that are yellow or white have much earth; and those that are black have much water."

There are four masters of lightning: Śarīrasvāda in the east, Śatapati in the south, Akṣara in the west, and Aśvalāna in the north; because these four lightnings contend with one another, there is thunder. Furthermore, because water, fire, wind, and earth contend with one another, there is thunder.
"There are five reasons for there being no rain:

first, when wind arises and blows; second, when fire arises and scorches; third, when the asuras take it up with their hands and cast it into the sea; fourth, when the rain-masters engage in licentiousness; and fifth, when the king does not govern properly, and because the rain-masters are angry, they do not send rain," and so forth.
"Simultaneously pouring down" and below is the fourth, the analogy of pouring rain.
This illustrates how, by means of the eightfold voice and four analytical knowledges of the secret mouth, the rain of the Dharma is proclaimed and poured down to benefit and nourish sentient beings.
Regarding the phrase "its moisture universally permeates" below, this is the fifth analogy, that of moistening and nourishing.

The Dharma-treasure rains universally upon the seeds of the causes of habitual practice within the minds of the seven types of sentient beings; these immediately give rise to the wisdom of hearing (*śrutamayī-prajñā*), which is termed "moistening and permeating."

Regarding "branches, leaves, roots, and stems": faith is the root, precepts are the stem, concentration is the branch, and wisdom is the leaf; because they mutually support one another in this sequence, these four are used as a metaphor.

The small roots and stems, etc., refer to the faith and precepts of humans and devas; the medium roots and stems, etc., refer to the faith and precepts of the two vehicles; and the great roots and stems, etc., refer to the faith and precepts of bodhisattvas.

Below the passage "All trees, large and small," is the sixth section, the analogy of growth. This further briefly restates that vegetation receives moisture according to its respective capacity; likewise, once the two causes—habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and retribution (*vipāka*)—and the wholesome dharmas have received the rain of the Dharma, the two fruits—habitual tendencies and retribution—each attain growth.

"According to their spiritual disposition" clarifies that the employment of skillful means accords with the capacities of beings: for those of the Lesser Vehicle, there is no excess; for those of the Greater Vehicle, there is no deficiency. This refers precisely to the seven kinds of causes, consisting of both the causal and resultant conditions.
The phrase "flowers, fruits, and ripened seeds" refers to the two types of fruition: the fruition of practice (*śikṣā-phala*) and the fruition of retribution (*vipāka-phala*).
Furthermore, it is said that "increase" (*vṛddhi*) has three meanings: being in accordance with one's spiritual lineage (*gotra*) is the cause of increase;
because the establishment of the teaching accords with the capacities of sentient beings, each attains increase—this precisely clarifies the meaning of increase.
"The flourishing of flowers and fruits" is the sign of growth.
From the passage "Though born from the same earth" onwards is the second major section: the analogy of no distinction between one earth and one rain, which reveals the single reality (*eka-tattva*).
This has three aspects:
first, that which arises from a single ground—arising from the ground of the mind prior to the Path, yet ultimately resulting from the ground of wisdom after the Path;

second, that which is rained down by a single cloud and proclaimed by a single voice—the Dharma-gate of the One Vehicle—which develops the five kinds of roots of goodness within the Path, and is ultimately the teaching of equality through a single voice.

Third, the three types of grass and two types of trees receive benefit without being aware of it; likewise, those with the five kinds of roots of goodness receive the rain of the Buddha-dharma and grow according to their respective capacities without being aware of it. These five causes all rely upon the single Buddha-nature, yet they do not know this. Furthermore, they do not know that the teachings of the five vehicles are all Mahāyāna, nor do they know that they all ultimately return to the Buddha-wisdom; only the Tathāgata can know this.
"Kāśyapa, you should know that the Tathāgata... and so forth, below, is the application of the parables (*upasaṃhāra*). The application of the distinct parables is twofold:
first, the formal application; second, the restatement of the parables to apply them.
There are six types of analogies for differentiation; here they are combined and presented out of sequence.

The opening analogies clarify the capacity (*indriya*) and precede the discussion of sentient beings, while the closing analogies clarify the response (*prativyāhāra*) and precede the application to the Tathāgata, who is the master of transformation.
Among these, the first corresponds primarily to the third [analogy] above, the dense clouds, while it also concurrently corresponds to the first world;
the second here corresponds to the fourth above, the analogy of pouring rain;
and the third here corresponds to the first above, the analogy of the mountains, rivers, streams, and valleys of the world.
Among these, the fourth corresponds to the second [analogy] above regarding grasses and trees;
the fifth corresponds to the fifth above regarding moistening;
and the sixth corresponds to the sixth above regarding growth.

Regarding the sequence of the analogies: it clarifies that when the Tathāgata appears in the world, he preaches the Dharma with the eight qualities of his voice; when he preaches the Dharma, there are sentient beings who receive transformation through it; and when these sentient beings hear the Dharma, each is moistened by the Way. While they are identical in receiving this moisture, there are no differences in their subsequent growth, and so forth.
First, the union with the secret cloud.
First, the Buddha’s body-secret is raised to correspond to the cloud having form;
subsequently, the Buddha’s speech-secret is raised to correspond to the cloud having sound.
“The Tathāgata likewise appears in the world in this same manner” precisely corresponds to the appearance of the *sambhogakāya* (enjoyment body) in the world.
“Like the rising of a great cloud” is the illustrative metaphor used for correspondence, clarifying that the Tathāgata’s great compassion manifests in form to cover and nourish all beings.
"By means of a great voice" refers to citing the Buddha’s secret of speech (*vāg-guhyaka*), which corresponds to the clouds possessing sound.

"Devas, humans, and asuras" specifically cites the three virtuous realms who receive the benefit of the secret of speech; that is to say, the thirty sons of the three vehicles’ spiritual capacities, who individually receive the benefit of the sound.
"Like that great cloud" is the citation of the simile, which corresponds to the fact that the cloud possesses sound.
"Pervading and covering the trichiliocosm" refers generally to all beings as sons of the Buddha, who together receive the benefit of the Buddha’s secret of speech (*vāgguhya*).
Alternatively, one may combine only five analogies, taking the phrase "pervading the world" and below to include the lands of the world as well.

The "world" refers to the world of physical environments (bhājanaloka), while "gods, humans, and asuras" refers to the world of sentient beings (sattvaloka) as the conventional designation of the five aggregates (pañcaskandha). The conventional designation corresponds to the aforementioned "world," and the five aggregates correspond to the mountains, rivers, and valleys.
The passage beginning with "proclaiming amidst the great assembly" constitutes the second section, which corresponds to the fourth preceding illustration of raining down [the Dharma].
First, the topical headings are set forth; next, the audience is exhorted to listen and accept.
There are six topical headings:
first, the ten titles, namely "Tathāgata, Arhat," and so forth;
second, the four great vows, namely "to cause those not yet delivered to be delivered," and so forth.
Third, the three types of penetration (*trividya*), referring to "the present world and future worlds," and so forth;
fourth, the three knowledges within a single mind (*ekacitta-trijñāna*), referring to "the one who possesses complete knowledge";
fifth, the five eyes (*pañcacakṣus*), referring to "the one who sees."

Sixth, the three karmas act in conjunction with wisdom: "knowing the path" refers to non-restraint of the mind; "opening the path" refers to non-restraint of the body; and "expounding the path" refers to non-restraint of speech. They are also called "guides," meaning those who know the path and so forth.
The passage beginning with "You, gods and humans" exhorts all beings to listen and receive [the teaching].

The Buddha’s eightfold voice articulates six kinds of Dharma gates; speaking from the perspective of what is most prevalent, he exhorts them toward the three wholesome paths, and thus one ought to go and listen to the Dharma.
From "At that time, there were countless billions of kinds" up to "and listen to the Dharma," this third section corresponds to the first analogy of mountains and rivers above.
Sentient beings exist by gathering together their karmic retributions, just as the world and its various features come into being based upon mountains and rivers.
"Billions" refers to the sentient beings of the ten dharma realms.
Here, we are specifically discussing the distinctions among the sentient beings of the seven stages of expedient means, which correspond to what was explained above.
The passage beginning with "Whether you gods or humans" harmonizes with the analogy of the mountains and rivers.
The section from "At that time, the Tathāgata... up to "...diligent or indolent" constitutes the fourth [analogy], which corresponds to the second analogy above regarding the grasses and trees.
The old commentary states:
"This passage is an expansion that does not correspond to what precedes it.

Now, I clarify that in the preceding analogy, there were differences among the plants and trees in terms of their size; here, it clarifies that roots have varying degrees of sharpness or dullness and practices have varying degrees of progress or stagnation. This precisely concerns the depth of the causal conditions for cultivation, which is identical in meaning to the analogy of the plants and trees. How could this not be a correspondence to the analogy, rather than an expansion?

Regarding the phrase "at that time": if one discusses the very beginning of the gradual process, it refers to the time when the Three Vehicles were first taught at the Deer Park; if one discusses the intermediate period, "at that time" may be applied to various instances throughout.

Regarding "sharpness and dullness": as a general judgment, those in the three miserable realms—who due to their evil causes experience bitter fruits and are unable to receive the Way—are termed "dull"; those who, through the seven kinds of expedient means, gain benefit upon hearing the teaching are termed "sharp. As a specific judgment, humans and devas who merely receive retributive fruits and are unwilling to receive the Way are termed "dull," while those of the three vehicles whose faculties sever delusions and transcend the realms are termed "sharp.
Furthermore, Śrāvakas who contemplate arising and ceasing are termed "dull," while Bodhisattvas who contemplate non-arising and non-ceasing are termed "sharp.
This applies likewise to the Shared, Distinct, and Perfect [teachings], and so forth.

Heedlessness in the three miserable realms is called "laziness" (*kausīdya*); for humans and devas, observing the five precepts and the ten wholesome paths is "diligence," while not being weary of suffering as humans and devas is "laziness"; for those of the two vehicles, fearing impermanence is "diligence," while craving realization and failing to seek Buddhahood is "laziness"; and for Bodhisattvas, aspiring to seek the Buddha-way is "progression" (*vīrya*), and so forth.

From "according to their capacity" (*yathābhavyatayā*) to "swiftly obtaining great benefit," this constitutes the fifth section, which combines with the preceding to form the fifth analogy of being moistened by the rain.
"According to their capacity" means that [the teaching] accords with the suitability of the faculties, free from the faults of excess or deficiency.
"Rejoicing, they obtain a wholesome benefit" means that each receives the nourishment and benefit of the Dharma.
"When these sentient beings have heard this Dharma" is the sixth point, which corresponds to the sixth analogy above regarding growth.

"Peace and security in the present life and rebirth in a good realm" refers to the retributive cause (*vipāka-hetu*) producing its retributive fruit (*vipāka-phala*), which corresponds to the growth of the blossoming flowers.

"Furthermore, one attains hearing of the Dharma," up to "entering the Path," refers to the habitual cause (*abhyāsa-hetu*) drawing forth its habitual fruit (*abhyāsa-phala*), which corresponds to the growth of the ripened fruit.

"Having heard this Dharma" corresponds to the cause for increase; "peace and security in the present life" precisely corresponds to the increase itself; and "rebirth in a good realm in future lives" corresponds to the signs of that increase.

The Buddha is like a great cloud that universally covers all; even those in the three miserable realms receive its moistening and attain growth. As it is said in the *Prajñāpāramitā* and other Vaipulya sutras, that those in the hells likewise obtain benefit.
Furthermore, various sutras also state that dragons, birds, ghosts, spirits, and others hear the Dharma and attain the Way.
If the fire is extinguished and the boiling water cools, this constitutes peace and security in the present life;
if they are reborn among devas or humans, this constitutes a favorable rebirth in a future life.
To cultivate the Path among devas and humans is itself to experience happiness through the Path.
If humans or devas hear the Dharma, uphold the precepts, and have their bodies sustained by merit, they will not be harmed by ghosts or nāgas; this is peace and security in the present life.
Whether they are reborn as devas or reborn as humans, or whether devas and humans are reborn interchangeably, this constitutes birth in a favorable realm in future lives.
To be able to awaken to and understand this is precisely to receive joy through the Way.

When those of the Two Vehicles hear the Dharma, they attain *nirvāṇa* with remainder; this is peace and security in the present life. As the text below states: "This person conceives the thought of having attained extinction regarding the merits they have acquired," and "I shall become a Buddha in another land under a different name. This person, hearing this sutra in that land, regards that land of skillful means with remainder as a virtuous place; hearing the sutra there constitutes receiving joy through the Way.

If a bodhisattva in an embodied state hears the Dharma preached by Vairocana Buddha and attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), they will find peace and security in the present life; in future lives, they will be born in the world of Pure Fulfillment as members of the retinue of the Dharma-body. To dwell in such a virtuous place and experience bliss through the Way, free from all obstacles, is what constitutes peace and security in the present life.
"Entering the Way gradually according to one's capacity" means that in future lives one will experience happiness through the Way.

As for the "Five Vehicles": the Vehicle of the Five Precepts delivers one from the suffering of the three miserable realms; the Vehicle of the Ten Wholesome Deeds delivers one from the eight sufferings of the human realm; the Śrāvaka Vehicle delivers one from the suffering of impermanence within the triple world; the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle delivers one from the suffering of hearing the Dharma from others; and the Bodhisattva Vehicle delivers one from the suffering of lacking internal wisdom and external marks of excellence—these constitute the Five Vehicles.
Question:
Should it not be the case that only the vehicles of humans and devas constitute the mundane vehicle (*laukika-yāna*), while the others are supramundane vehicles (*lokottara-yāna*)?
Furthermore, should not the Buddha’s vehicle be the ultimate vehicle (*tattvika-yāna*), while the others are provisional vehicles (*upāyika-yāna*)?
Furthermore, the Buddha is the vehicle of the fruit, while the others are the vehicles of the cause.
Moreover, there should be three vehicles: humans and devas as the lower, the two vehicles as the middle, and the Buddha as the superior.

Furthermore, humans and devas are called the vehicle that does not sever afflictions; the two vehicles are called the vehicle that severs afflictions; and the Buddha is called the vehicle that neither severs nor does not sever [afflictions].
Moreover, humans and devas are called "not severing," the Buddha is called "severing," and the two vehicles are called "both severing and not severing."

Furthermore, there are various vehicles such as those for ordinary persons, noble ones, and those who are neither ordinary nor noble; existence, emptiness, and that which is neither existent nor empty, and so forth.

How do these relate to the five roots of goodness clarified in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, the four treasuries distinguished in the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, and the three types of grass and two types of trees?

Human and celestial beings constitute two [vehicles] of goodness; the Two Vehicles constitute one; Buddhas and Bodhisattvas constitute five. This is the opening of the Great and the closing of the Small. When the Great is opened and the Small is closed, the Four Baskets (Catuḥpiṭaka) close off the ordinary and open up the holy. In the Five Vehicles, both the ordinary and the holy are opened; they differ only according to conditions.

Regarding the section beginning with "Like that great cloud," the second part provides a summary by correlating the six points through analogy: "The great cloud" correlates with the first point, the dual benefit of form and sound;
"raining upon all" correlates with the second point, the six chapters of the Dharma-gate;

and "the herbs, trees, and forests" correlate with the fourth point, the varying capacities—sharp or dull, diligent or indolent—of the sentient beings receiving transformation, as well as the depth or shallowness of their causal practice.
"According to their respective lineages, they fully receive nourishment" corresponds to the fifth [point], receiving nourishment and attaining the benefit of the Dharma;
"each attains growth" corresponds to the sixth, the increase of peace and security in the present life.
"Below the passage 'The Tathāgata teaches the Dharma with a single characteristic' is the second section, which synthesizes the analogies of non-differentiation.
Above, three [analogies] were opened; now, three are likewise synthesized, though not in the same order."
From "one mark and one flavor" downward, the single ground and the single rain are unified.
From "that which is called" downward, the single ground and the single rain are explained together.
From "if there are sentient beings" downward, this corresponds to the previous point that although all grasses and trees each have their differences.
The section beginning with "For what reason? explains the distinction: the Tathāgata is able to know both distinction and non-distinction.
"One characteristic" means that the minds of sentient beings share the same characteristic of True Suchness (tathatā); this is the "one ground."
"Single flavor" means that the Dharma of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) equally elucidates a single principle; this is the "single rain.

In the past, through skillful means, the one true reality was opened into seven aspects; within the Dharma of the One Vehicle, it was distinguished and taught as seven teachings. The Buddha knows that they ultimately all return to the single aspect and single flavor.
The section beginning with "That which is called" provides a dual explanation of the single characteristic and the single flavor.

The nature of the sentient beings' minds is itself the nature-endowment (*dharmatā-guṇa*), consisting of the three characteristics of liberation, detachment, and cessation. When the Tathāgata speaks these three dharmas with a single voice, they constitute the three flavors; these three characteristics serve as the practice of the Middle Way arising from conditions within the objective realm, ultimately resulting in the fruit of all-knowledge. Therefore, it is said that "one ultimately reaches all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*)."
The analogy of the distinctions among grasses and trees will not be recorded again here, as it will be explained later.
At times, the analogy is applied with three meanings:
first, the meaning of non-distinction, which corresponds to the single earth and the single rain of the preceding section.
2. The meaning of differentiation: this combines with the preceding [point on] the differentiation between grasses and trees;

3. The Tathāgata’s ability to know: this explains that the two meanings are without differentiation, namely, the single characteristic and the single flavor. "Single characteristic" combines with the preceding [point on] the first stage (*bhūmi*).
The "characteristic of liberation" means the absence of the characteristics of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).
The "characteristic of detachment" means the absence of the characteristic of nirvāṇa.

The "characteristic of cessation" means that there is neither the characteristic of having characteristics nor the characteristic of being without characteristics; because there is only the true characteristic (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), it is called the "one characteristic. This one characteristic is the foundation of non-abiding from which all dharmas are established. Non-abiding and the absence of characteristics constitute non-differentiation.
The establishment of all phenomena involves differentiation;
differentiation is like various herbs and trees, while non-differentiation is like the single earth.
Although the earth itself has no differentiation, it can produce the various differences of peaches, plums, herbs, and trees.
Although peaches, apricots, and various plants and trees differ from one another, they are all equally characterized by solidity.
If one knows that the earth possesses the peaches and apricots, one recognizes that within the real there is the provisional; one understands that non-differentiation is itself differentiation.
If one knows the solid nature of the peaches and apricots, one recognizes that within the provisional there is the real; one understands that differentiation is itself non-differentiation.
For this reason, the analogy of the upper stage is joined with the single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*).
"Single flavor" (*ekarasa*) refers to the true teaching that is pure, unitary, and without admixture; by extension, the single characteristic can be understood in the same way.
"Emancipation" refers to being free from the karmic bonds of the two extremes—fragmentation and transformation; thus it is called the "characteristic of emancipation.

"Detachment from characteristics" refers to attaining the wisdom of the Middle Way; because this wisdom can remain far removed from the two extremes and is without attachment, it is called "detachment from characteristics."

Regarding the "characteristic of cessation": because the cessation of the causes of the two extremes results in *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, and the cessation of the fruits of the two extremes results in *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, it is called the "characteristic of cessation."
Every phrase serves as an illustration of the meaning of "difference yet non-differentiation";

this can be understood by analogy with the "one mark. Regarding the phrase "ultimately reaching all-knowledge" (*sarvākārajñatā*): if one attains the cessation of the two extremes, this constitutes the exhaustion of both the common and specific delusions, entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision. One practices *prajñā* within the mind of all-knowledge; because the initial aspiration and the ultimate consummation are not distinct, it is called "ultimate. This is precisely the wisdom of the Buddha, hence it is termed "all-knowledge."
Regarding the passage, "There are sentient beings who hear the Tathāgata’s Dharma but do not realize it for themselves," this clarifies the meaning of differentiation.

From here on, the following clarifies these distinctions: "sentient beings" refers to the distinction between the provisional and the real, such as mountains and rivers, as well as the distinction of seeds; "the Tathāgata" is the cloud; "hearing the Dharma" is the rain; "reciting and practicing" is the moisture; and "merit" is the growth. [These beings] are unable to understand any such distinctions.
The text is divided into five sections:

first, sentient beings do not know; second, the Tathāgata is able to know; third, an analogy is presented and applied to the fact that sentient beings do not know; fourth, the preceding point is restated to conclude and explain how the Tathāgata is able to know; fifth, the resolution of doubts.
The phrase "there are sentient beings" refers to those who do not know.
"Dharma" refers to hearing the Dharma of a single sound; "retaining and expounding it" precisely clarifies their lack of knowledge.

Their upholding and exposition differ, and their practices vary: those of the human and celestial realms form an understanding of precepts and wholesome deeds, while those of the Three Vehicles form an understanding of the Truths, the Conditions, and the Perfections; since these understandings differ, they constitute distinctions.

Regarding the phrase "the merit attained is not self-aware," this clarifies that although the five groups of people each received the teaching, they did not know that the Buddha’s teaching was of a single flavor without distinction, nor did they understand the seven kinds of skillful means. Each formed their own interpretations and clung to their own understanding as the truth; thus, they neither knew the provisional nor recognized the real—this is precisely what is meant by "not being self-aware of the distinctions."
Second, the Tathāgata is able to know.
To summarize the enumeration and cite ten objects, these are combined into four points:
first, knowing by means of four dharmas; second, knowing by means of three dharmas; third, knowing by means of two dharmas; and fourth, being able to know by means of one dharma.
Regarding the summary of the four dharmas, they are: seed (*bīja*), characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), essence (*svabhāva*), and nature (*dhātu*).

As for "seed," the three paths are the seeds of the three virtues. The *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states: "The entire host of afflictions constitutes the seed of the Tathāgata. This clarifies that through the path of affliction, there is precisely prajñā.
Furthermore, it is said that "the five *ānantarya* [sins] all give rise to the appearance of liberation"; this means that from within the unwholesome, there is the wholesome dharma of liberation.
All sentient beings are themselves the appearance of *nirvāṇa* and cannot be further extinguished; this is precisely the taking of birth-and-death as the *dharmakāya*.

This is discussed from the perspective of relative categories; however, if discussed from the perspective of universal categories, every instance of bowing the head or raising the hand is a seed of liberation. All worldly wisdom and the minds of the three vehicles that seek liberation are seeds of *prajñā*. Indeed, all who possess a mind shall become Buddhas—this is the seed of the *dharmakāya*. The Tathāgata is able to know these various distinctions among the seeds.
Yet, all seeds are in fact but a single seed, which is non-differentiation; the Tathāgata is likewise able to know this.
That differentiation is non-differentiation, and non-differentiation is differentiation—the Tathāgata is likewise able to know this.
Characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), essence (*tattva*), and nature (*svabhāva*) are explained in terms of the ten dharma-realms (*dharmadhātu*) and the ten suchnesses (*tathatā*).
If one discusses their differentiation, they are the characteristics of the ten dharma-realms; if one discusses their non-differentiation, they are the characteristic of the single Buddha-realm.
The Tathāgata is able to know distinction and non-distinction;
that distinction is itself non-distinction and non-distinction is itself distinction—the Tathāgata is likewise able to know this.
The principles regarding essence (*tattva*) and nature (*prakṛti*) may be understood by analogy.
From the section "What is recollected" onwards, the Tathāgata’s capacity for knowledge is elucidated by way of three dharmas.
These three dharmas are the three types of wisdom (prajñā), which further comprise three levels:
first, the objects of the three wisdoms; second, the essence of the three wisdoms; and third, the causes and conditions of the three wisdoms.
Contemplating what object constitutes the application of the three types of wisdom (*prajñā*).
Taking up the object of contemplation is precisely the sphere of the three wisdoms.
Regarding "how one contemplates": contemplation is the recording of the Dharma as it has been heard; this is the very essence of the wisdom of mindfulness (*smṛti-prajñā*).

From the section beginning with "By means of what dharma does one recollect," it follows that the three types of wisdom (trividya) apprehending their objects—namely, hearing the Dharma—is their causal condition (*pratyaya*).

Furthermore, because the objects and the wisdoms of these three types of wisdom conjoin as causal conditions, the dharmas of the three types of wisdom come to exist; thus, they are further termed "causal conditions."
Regarding these three vehicles and their three types of wisdom, it was previously held that there is a distinction because the objects, essences, and causes and conditions differ;
however, upon entering the perfect and subtle threefold wisdom, there is no longer any distinction.
The Tathāgata is able to know these distinctions and non-distinctions;
furthermore, that distinction is itself non-distinction, and non-distinction is itself distinction—the Tathāgata is likewise able to know this.
From the phrase "By what dharma" onwards, the Tathāgata’s capacity for knowledge is elucidated in terms of two dharmas.
"By what dharma" refers to the cause, while "attaining what dharma" refers to the fruit.

The various causes of the five vehicles each obtain their respective fruits; this constitutes differentiation. Yet, the suchness of sentient beings is the suchness of the Buddha, and this single suchness is non-dual suchness; it is solely a single cause and a single fruit, which is thus without differentiation.
The Tathāgata is also able to know distinction and non-distinction;
he is also able to know that distinction is itself non-distinction and non-distinction is itself distinction.
From the phrase "sentient beings dwell in various stages," it is understood that the Tathāgata is able to know this in terms of a single dharma.
The seven stages of expedient means abide in seven positions; therefore, they are called "various grounds," which refers to their differentiation.
When the Tathāgata perceives them with his Buddha-eye of suchness, they are like the various rivers flowing into the sea and losing their original flavors—then there is no differentiation.
When he expounds speech according to the intentions of others through the skillful means of wisdom, the Tathāgata is able to know their distinctions;
when the teachings he proclaims all reach the stage of omniscience, the Tathāgata is able to know their non-distinction, and so forth.
From "Just as those herbs and trees" onwards is the third section, which provides an analogy and applies it to show that sentient beings do not know [this].
From "The Tathāgata knows this" onwards is the fourth section, which restates the preceding points to summarize his capacity for knowledge.
"Single characteristic and single flavor," and so forth, are explained as before.
"Single characteristic and single flavor," "liberation," "separation," "cessation," and so on, when analyzed through conditions, constitute the infinite within the one;
"ultimate nirvana ultimately returns to emptiness" constitutes the one within the infinite.
This restates the previous point to re-explain the absence of differentiation. Why?

Such terms as "one mark," "one flavor," "liberation," "separation," and "extinction"—if these were the essential nature of the Dharma of the Two Vehicles—would still be declarations of differentiation. Now, by establishing that Mahāyāna ultimate nirvāṇa ultimately returns to emptiness, it universally accords with the absence of differentiation.

"Ultimate Nirvana" concludes that the preceding phrases do not refer to the *sopadhiśeṣa* (with remainder) or *nirupadhiśeṣa* (without remainder) nirvana of the two vehicles, but rather to ultimate nirvana.
Regarding "the mark of eternal quiescence," this concludes that the various phrases do not refer to the quiescence of the Lesser Vehicle, but rather to the eternally abiding quiescence.
The preceding passage states, "All dharmas from the very beginning are eternally characterized by quiescence"; this is precisely that meaning.

As for "ultimately returning to emptiness," this is not the emptiness of annihilationism, but rather the emptiness of the primary truth of the Middle Way—a solemn and emphatic realization of the distinction between the ultimate reality and provisional means.

Regarding the old saying that "one ultimately returns to emptiness": although one may manifest the extension of life through supernatural powers for immeasurable eons, doubling even the aforementioned numbers, when the lifespan is exhausted, one ultimately returns to the cessation of ashes; therefore, it is said that one ultimately returns to emptiness.
Regarding this *Sūtra on the Buddha’s Suffering*, how can it be described?
Guangzhai said:
"In the end, one returns to entering the realm of *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, casting off the impermanent body and [retaining] wisdom."
Someone raises an objection to this interpretation: "If that is so, how does this differ from the Two Vehicles? The sutra text mentions two forms of culmination:
the first is culminating in all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*); this cites the fruit of wisdom as being non-culminative when contrasted with the wisdom of the Two Vehicles.

The second is culminating in *nirvāṇa*, the eternally quiescent mark that ultimately returns to emptiness; this cites the abandonment [of defilements] as being non-culminative when contrasted with the abandonment of the Two Vehicles."
The ultimate text makes it clear that this is not the emptiness of the Hīnayāna. Longyin stated:

"The emptiness of the Mahāparinirvāṇa is called 'emptiness' because there is neither the mark of dharmas nor afflictions; it ultimately returns to the eternally abiding emptiness of the primary meaning (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*)."
Master Zhong said:
"In the end, it all returns to the wisdom of the primary emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
Someone else said: "Because the Buddha’s fruition is free from all attachments, it is called empty."
The commentator says:
"Only when emptiness thoroughly dispels existence is it called 'emptiness.
None of the ancient masters provided such a minor interpretation; for what reason did Guangzhai alone do so?"
"Having known this, the Buddha observes sentient beings," and so forth; this is the fifth [section], which eliminates the doubts of others. [The questioner asks:
Since the Buddha already knew from the beginning that the beginning and the end are one and the same, why did he not preach the Truth immediately at the Deer Park?

The commentary states: "Observing the desires of the minds of sentient beings, he protects them in accordance with the three *siddhāntas*; fearing they might slander [the teaching], he does not speak immediately.
From the passage "You, O Kāśyapa," onwards is the second section, which returns to the core doctrine and provides a description to resolve doubts.
As for those who harbor doubts: having heard of the Buddha’s immeasurable merits, they wonder whether the four disciples’ simultaneous realization through the teaching must necessarily be real.
Therefore, the Buddha stated that although they had not yet reached the stage of Buddhahood, their simultaneous realization through the teaching was not false.
This also serves to inspire those of inferior faculties, enabling them to attain awakening together.
The text is divided into two parts:
first, the statement; second, the explanation.

First, regarding the praise of "rareness": ordinary beings possess a tendency toward regression, yet they can gain benefit upon hearing [the teaching]; for Bodhisattvas, who have already understood these matters and do not find them particularly marvelous, it is truly rare that they are able to renounce and enter the realization of the unconditioned state of true reality (*asaṃskṛta-bhūmi*). Next, the ability to know how to preach the Dharma according to what is appropriate describes their capacity to lead others; the subsequent statement regarding their ability to believe and accept describes their realization and reveals the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

"Why is this so? This phrase explains the underlying intention, clarifying that while the Buddha speaks of three [vehicles] within a single path, it is profound, mysterious, and difficult to understand that you are nonetheless able to believe it.

In my private view, the preceding text states, "The Tathāgata further possesses immeasurable merits that you cannot fully describe," while the subsequent text says, "You are truly rare. The Buddha’s grace universally covers all, like clouds and rain that moisten everything without exception; the Buddha’s grace universally sustains all, like the great earth that brings all things to life and growth. How could it be intended for only a single capacity or a single region? Therefore, it is said that you cannot fully describe it.

Although the Buddha’s grace is universal, sentient beings do not realize it in their daily lives; they are like the three types of grass and two types of trees that take root in the earth and receive nourishment from the rain, yet remain unaware of it. That you are able to recognize these tenfold graces from beginning to end is truly rare.
"Those not yet liberated, I shall cause to be liberated," and so forth—this describes his knowledge of the Buddha’s grace of the Four Great Vows, which is most rare.

"May sentient beings find peace and security in the present life, be reborn in good realms in future lives, and experience happiness through the Way"—this describes his knowledge of the grace of great compassion that bestows happiness, which is most rare.

Having heard the Dharma, they are freed from all obstacles and, according to their capacity, gradually enter the Path; thus they express their awareness of the kindness of Great Compassion in uprooting suffering, which is truly rare.

The Wheel-turning Kings, Śakra, and Brahmā are like minor medicinal herbs; it is most rare that they are described as knowing how to exhort others toward goodness and thus remove the heat of affliction.

Those who know the untainted dharmas (anāsrava-dharma) capable of attaining nirvāṇa and the realization of a pratyekabuddha are like intermediate medicinal herbs; it is most rare that they are described as knowing how to remove all the heat of views and craving.

The small tree growing atop [the large one] represents being ashamed of one's own smallness and admiring the greatness of others; it describes the grace of knowing how to conceal one's ugliness, which is truly rare.
The large tree represents the grace of majestic adornment, which is truly rare.

Regarding the single ground and single rain of the most ultimate reality, it describes the exceedingly rare grace of knowing how to bestow the seat and the treasury, and how to bring about the sovereign peace and bliss of body, mind, wealth, and Dharma.
When the Buddha describes its differentiated aspects in his praise, the text for praising the ten kinds of grace is exhausted;
however, if he describes its undifferentiated aspect, it is simply this one great grace.
The verses consist of fifty-four and a half lines, which provide a metrical commentary on the preceding exposition.
This exposition contains both the doctrine and its analogies, all of which are now versified.
The first four lines verse the doctrinal explanation (*dharmadeśanā*).
The following fifty lines and a half are in verse, providing an illustrative explanation.
This explanatory section on the Dharma is further divided into two parts: first, the presentation of the Dharma King; second, the revelation and elucidation.
Now, the first half-verse praises the non-falsity of the Dharma King;
the following three and a half lines praise the revelation and manifestation.
The two teachings and two wisdoms mentioned in the preceding text are likewise fully praised here.
The first one and a half lines praise the two teachings;
the latter two lines praise the two wisdoms.
Within this, the second half-line of the first verse, "according to sentient beings," praises the provisional teaching.
Next, from "The Tathāgata’s Veneration" downward, the second section consists of one line, which praises the teaching of reality (*bhūtadharmadeśanā*).
Next, from "If one with wisdom hears this" downward, the next line praises the explanation of provisional wisdom (*upāyajñāna*);
finally, from "Therefore, Kāśyapa" downward, the next line praises the explanation of ultimate wisdom (*bhūtajñāna*).
Teaching various doctrines according to various conditions is entirely for the purpose of enabling one to attain the correct view of the Mahāyāna;
prior to this, all are termed wrong views. This verse expresses the intent of the Tathāgata’s four *siddhāntas*:

"The Dharma King who destroys existence" refers to the *prātipakṣika-siddhānta* (the therapeutic intent); "according to the desires of sentient beings" refers to the *lokasaṃvṛti-siddhānta* (the worldly intent); "wisdom, hearing, faith, understanding, and the eternal loss of doubt and regret" constitute the *puruṣa-siddhānta* (the personal intent); and "enabling one to attain correct view" is the *paramārtha-siddhānta* (the ultimate intent).

The three *siddhāntas* correspond to the preceding verse on "expounding through the skillful means of wisdom" to enable the attainment of right view; they correspond to the preceding verse on "reaching the stage of all-knowledge," and so forth.
The section beginning with "Kāśyapa, you should know that it is like... and extending for fifty and a half lines, corresponds to the preceding section of parables.
The first ten and a half lines constitute the verses on the opening of the analogies;
the subsequent forty lines constitute the verses on the application of the analogies.
Above, two analogies were opened; now, for the first time, nine and a half stanzas provide the verses on the analogy of differentiation.
The next line praises the analogy of non-differentiation.
Above, there were six points of differentiation; now, six are likewise praised, yet they do not expand upon the analogies as in the prose section, following instead the order of their synthesis.
The first three lines of the verse praise the third simile of the clouds;
the second section, "Its rain is universal and equal," consisting of one line, praises the fourth simile of pouring down rain;
next, from "Mountains, rivers, and steep valleys" onwards, the third section, consisting of one line, praises the first simile of the land, mountains, and rivers.
Next, following "profound and remote," the fourth section consists of two lines, which eulogize the second simile of the grasses and trees;
next, following "various large and small trees," the fifth section consists of two lines and three phrases, which eulogize the fifth simile of receiving moisture;
and following "all the various trees," the sixth section consists of two lines, which eulogize the sixth simile of growth.
The clouds are a metaphor for the response-body (nirmāṇakāya); because the response-body acts in accordance with wisdom, it is called "the cloud of wisdom.
Because it can fully possess the twelve divisions of the Dharma, it is said to be "moistening and nourishing."
If the response-body (nirmāṇakāya) were not to preach the Dharma—just as in the cases of Suśānta and Prabhūtaratna—then these clouds would lack moisture.
Its body emits great radiance like "flashing lightning," and its mouth vibrates with the four analytical knowledges (pratisaṃvid) like "thunder."

Because the ninety-five kinds of false radiance do not appear, it is said that they are "obscured"; because the ninety-eight kinds of afflictive heat are removed, it is like the "coolness upon the ground."

Regarding the phrase "as if it could be grasped": the response-body (nirmāṇakāya) descends into the world appearing as if identical to the three realms of existence; though one may have the intention to grasp it, it is in fact unobtainable.

The eightfold voice and four types of eloquence proclaim and pour down the rain of Dharma; "falling everywhere at once" means it is heard simultaneously by all, which is also called the four immeasurables (catvāry apramāṇāni).
All who possess a mind receive its benefit; therefore, it is said that "the entire land is fully saturated.
This establishes the preceding point and also completes the analogy of the mountains and rivers below.

The phrase "mountains, rivers, and steep valleys" eulogizes the first [topic], the land; that is, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) of sentient beings within the seven stages of expedient means (*sapta-vidha-upāya*). Now, having received the rain of the Dharma, their bodies and speech become supple, just as the soil receives moisture.

"Born from what is profound and hidden" refers to the second point above: the differentiation of the causes of habituation among sentient beings. It is like the causes of habituation planted by sentient beings over a vast period of time, which remain concealed within the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense-bases (āyatanas); thus they are called "profound and hidden. Now, having encountered the rain of the Dharma, all are brought to full development; hence it is said they are "born [therefrom]."
The term "hundred grains" generally refers to the five grains, which serve as a metaphor for the five vehicles being able to produce a hundred kinds of goodness.
"Sugarcane and grapes" are metaphors for meditative concentration and wisdom.
"Thoroughly moistening dry land" is a metaphor for causing those who have not yet attained faith to believe.
The remainder is as in the prose.
The line beginning with “According to their substance, characteristics, nature, and divisions, whether large or small” constitutes the verse for the second analogy of non-differentiation.
In the preceding prose there were three points; here, the single ground (*ekabhūmi*) is omitted from the verse, yet what is produced therein is included therein as well.
The first two lines praise that which is produced and that which moistens;
the next line praises that which moistens, which is a praise of non-differentiation.
"Yet each flourishes luxuriantly" praises the lack of self-awareness regarding differentiation.
"‘The Buddha likewise appears in this way’" and the following forty lines constitute the second section, the combined analogy.
Of these, the first thirty-five verses combine the specific distinctions;
the subsequent five lines beginning with "In this way, Kāśyapa" combine the absence of distinction.

The superior correspondence with the analogies consists of a formal correspondence followed by an application of the analogy; now, this verse also first provides the correspondence and subsequently presents the analogy as an application.

The first line corresponds to the analogy of the clouds: the first two phrases correspond the body to the clouds, while the last two phrases present the analogy as an application of that correspondence.
Next, from "Having emerged" onwards, the second section consists of eight and a half lines, which versifies the second analogy of the rain.
First, the topical headings are presented; next, the audience is exhorted to listen and accept [the teaching].

The three lines following "Having emerged" briefly recite the ten epithets; the subsequent one and a half lines recite the four great vows. Among the six topical sections, only two sections are thus recited.
The one and a half lines beginning with “充潤一切” (saturating and moistening all) are a verse on the Four Great Vows.
The second section, consisting of four lines beginning with “諸天人” (all devas and humans), is a verse exhorting [the audience] to listen and receive [the teaching].
"From 'I observe all beings' below, the third section consists of four lines, forming a verse that combines the preceding metaphors of mountains and rivers.

The metaphor of mountains and rivers refers to sentient beings who possess the seven kinds of five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). Just as rain falls indiscriminately upon both valleys and peaks, the Buddha’s teaching is impartial; thus there is no distinction between "this" and "that. Those with the capacity for awakening are "this," while those without such capacity are "that. Planting roots of goodness is "love," while hatred and opposition are "hate. Buddha-activities are "self," while demonic activities are "other. Responding to the former is "coming," while responding to the latter is "going. Entering into reality is "sitting," while emerging in skillful means is "standing. The Buddha observes sentient beings in this manner; this is precisely the meaning of the equal rain falling upon mountains and rivers, and it corresponds to the previous verse describing how countless billions of kinds of sentient beings come to the Buddha’s presence to hear the Dharma."

"High and low, noble and base" (below): this fourth section consists of two lines and corresponds to the fourth [section] above, where the Tathāgata at that time contemplates these sentient beings; it combines with the second [section] regarding the grasses, trees, thickets, and forests that have grown.
From "noble or lowly" down to "sharp or dull," these are established through the successive stages of the seven preparatory practices (*saptavidha-prayoga*).

The section beginning with "All sentient beings who hear my Dharma" constitutes the fifth part; its eleven lines of verse summarize how all various and immeasurable [beings] are made to rejoice, corresponding to the analogy of receiving nourishment.
The text consists of three parts:
first, one line, which generally clarifies receiving the moisture;
